content: In physics, a quantum (plural: quanta) is an indivisible unit of a physical quantity that shares the same dimensions as Planck's constant. It is intrinsically linked to the energy and momentum of elementary particles, such as fermions (matter particles) and bosons (force-carrying particles, including photons). The term quantum originates from the Latin word quantus, meaning how much. This reflects the fundamental concept that certain physical properties are quantized, a phenomenon known as quantization. Quantization implies that these properties can only take on specific discrete values, rather than any value within a continuous range. A related concept is the quantum number, which describes these discrete states. For instance, a photon is often referred to as a light quantum. The energy of an electron bound to an atom is quantized, which is a key factor in the stability of atoms and matter as a whole. However, the term quantized can be misleading, as it refers to the quantization of Planck's constant, which can be expressed in units of energy multiplied by time or momentum multiplied by distance. Quantum mechanics, the branch of physics that deals with quantization, is widely regarded by physicists as the most fundamental framework for understanding and describing nature at the microscopic level. This is not a matter of human preference but rather a reflection of the intrinsic nature of the universe, as quantum mechanics consistently provides accurate predictions and explanations. The development of quantum theory began in 1900 when Max Planck introduced his theory to explain the emission spectrum of black bodies. In this work, Planck utilized a natural system of units he had devised the previous year. The differences between classical and quantum mechanics quickly became apparent, but it was not until 1926, through the efforts of Werner Heisenberg, Erwin Schrödinger, and others, that quantum mechanics was mathematically formalized and understood. Despite its experimental success, the philosophical interpretations of quantum theory remain a topic of debate. Planck himself was initially reluctant to accept the concept of quantization, as were many of his contemporaries. However, with no viable alternative, he continued to work with the idea, and his efforts were eventually recognized and celebrated. When he accepted the Nobel Prize in Physics 18 years later, he described the period of his initial work on quantization as a few weeks of the most strenuous work of his life, during which he had to abandon much of his earlier theoretical work. Quantization proved to be the only way to describe the new and detailed experimental findings emerging at the time. Planck openly shared his change of perspective with his scientific colleagues during meetings of the German Physical Society in late 1900, where black body radiation was a central topic of discussion. This marked the beginning of a significant scientific revolution. When a body is heated, it emits radiant heat, a form of electromagnetic radiation primarily in the infrared region of the spectrum. This phenomenon was well understood at the time and held considerable practical importance. As the body becomes hotter, it begins to emit visible light, starting with red wavelengths. However, most of the emitted radiation remains in the infrared until the body reaches extremely high temperatures, such as those on the surface of the Sun (approximately 6000°C), where the peak emission shifts to green light. At the time, laboratory conditions could not achieve such high temperatures, and the measurement of specific infrared wavelengths was only becoming feasible due to advancements in experimental techniques. Consequently, the detailed mapping of black body emission across the electromagnetic spectrum had not yet been accomplished. The quantum black-body radiation formula, the first piece of quantum mechanics, was derived by Planck on the evening of October 7, 1900, in what he described as a back-of-the-envelope calculation. This formula was based on the latest experimental findings in the infrared spectrum, reported to him by Heinrich Rubens. Planck sent the formula to Rubens on a postcard that same evening, and Rubens confirmed its accuracy a few days later. Initially, the formula was merely a fit to the experimental data, but it later revealed the necessity of quantization. Planck himself referred to this as a fortuitous guess at an interpolation formula. While refining the mathematics of his formula, Planck stumbled upon the foundations of quantum theory. He combined two mathematical expressions—one derived from earlier work on the red part of the spectrum and the other from the new infrared data—into a single formula. This formula accurately described the energy, ( E ), in a single mode of radiation at a given frequency, ( lambda ), and temperature, ( T ). The formula introduced two parameters, ( h ) (Planck's constant) and ( k ) (Boltzmann's constant), which are now fundamental constants in physics. At the time, however, their significance was not yet fully understood. The elementary quantum of energy is given by ( hlambda ), but such a unit does not normally exist and is not required for quantization. Although quantization was first discovered in the context of electromagnetic radiation, it describes a fundamental aspect of energy that is not limited to photons. From his experiments, Planck deduced the numerical values of ( h ) and ( k ), as well as other constants such as the Avogadro-Loschmidt number (the number of molecules in a mole) and the unit of electrical charge, with greater accuracy than previously known. He presented these findings at a meeting of the German Physical Society on December 14, 1900, marking the first revelation of energy quantization. This event is often referred to as the birth of quantum mechanics.
